title: Uniformly Stable Minimal Weyl--Heisenberg Measurements Approaching the SIC Benchmark
abstract: Informational completeness (IC) guarantees that an inverse exists, not that it is statistically well conditioned. For minimal rank-one Weyl--Heisenberg (WH) measurements, covariance makes the nonidentity projector-Gram spectrum proportional to the fiducial's ambiguity intensities, with eigenvalues \(d|χ_φ(u)|^2\), turning stability into an explicit worst-direction design problem; write \(λ\) for its smallest nonidentity eigenvalue. Haar fiducials are IC almost surely while \(\mathbb E[λ^{-1}]=\infty\), and an explicit geometric family used to establish balanced informationally complete measurements in every dimension has a normalized spectral floor bounded above by an exponentially decaying envelope. We then construct a hierarchy of minimal measurements. A cyclic family with exactly \(d^2\) outcomes in every integer dimension has floors \(Θ(d^{-3})\) for odd \(d\) and \(Θ(d^{-5})\) for even \(d\); a finite-field family for \(q=2^m\) obeys the uniform bound \(λ\ge4/9\). Our main result treats every prime-power dimension of characteristic \(p\ge5\). A balanced one-coordinate perturbation repairs the zero ambiguity axis of a cubic Alltop state, gives an attained floor uniformly bounded below by a positive constant, and confines the entire nonidentity spectrum to \([L_q,U_q]\) with \(U_q/L_q\to1\). Its SIC-normalized minimum tends to one, and \(λ(φ_q)/Λ_q^\star\to1\) for the global finite-field WH max--min optimum \(Λ_q^\star\), without assuming SIC existence. The complete spectrum determines the exact finite-sample Hilbert--Schmidt error of canonical linear inversion at \(I/d\), while its lower edge controls local Fisher efficiency and canonical-shadow bounds.
summary: This theoretical paper rigorously analyzes the spectral stability of Weyl--Heisenberg measurements relative to the ideal SIC benchmark. By developing explicit constructions in various dimensions (cyclic, finite-field), the authors derive quantitative lower bounds on the minimum eigenvalue ($\lambda$) and show that these measurements approach optimal performance asymptotically without requiring the existence of a true SIC state.
main_problem: The paper aims to quantify the spectral stability of minimal Weyl--Heisenberg (WH) measurements, determining how closely they can approach the ideal Symmetric Informationally Complete (SIC) benchmark without assuming SIC existence.
main_result: The authors construct a hierarchy of minimal measurements showing that for prime-power dimensions $p \ge 5$, perturbations of cubic Alltop states yield spectra confined to $[L_q, U_q]$ with the ratio $U_q/L_q$ approaching 1, and $\lambda(\phi_q)/\Lambda^\star_q 	o 1$.
method: The analysis heavily relies on spectral theory applied to the projector-Gram matrix derived from WH measurements, utilizing Fourier transforms, max-min optimization, and specialized algebraic techniques for cyclic and finite-field correlations.
model_or_system: The system under study is quantum measurement theory using minimal rank-one Weyl--Heisenberg (WH) measurements in a $d$-dimensional Hilbert space. The quality of the measurement is diagnosed via the spectrum of the Projector Gram matrix, $	ext{Spec}(G_\Pi^\phi)$.
key_observables: Smallest nonidentity eigenvalue ($\lambda(\phi)$), spectral stability measure ($\eta(\phi)$), and the canonical Mean-Squared Error ratio ($R(\phi)$).
important_parameters: Dimension $d$, prime power dimension $q=p^k$ with characteristic $p \ge 5$, and the SIC benchmark value.
main_assumptions: The analysis often proceeds by assuming specific algebraic structures (e.g., cyclic or finite-field settings) to derive bounds, though it aims to provide results without assuming exact SIC existence.
figures_summary: Figures compare spectral stability ($\eta$) across different dimensions and plot the exact MSE ratio ($R$) for canonical linear inversion against the WH-SIC benchmark ($R=1$).
paper_structure: The paper establishes the relationship between IC, uniform stability, and the SIC endpoint using the projector-Gram matrix spectrum. It then develops specific constructions (cyclic, finite-field) to derive quantitative bounds on $\lambda(\phi)$ and $\eta(\phi)$, culminating in results for prime-power dimensions.
why_interesting: This work provides rigorous, constructive methods to quantify measurement performance metrics like local Fisher efficiency and canonical error bounds, which are crucial for designing optimal quantum state tomography protocols.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Spectral stability beyond binary informational completeness; larger η is better. (a) A SIC is the exact η = 1 endpoint, uniform stability is a dimension-independent relative guarantee, and ordinary IC says only that the inverse exists, so conditioning may degrade. BIC is a tight minimal-IC structure, not a stability level. (b) Cyclic Z2 d benchmarks: blue shows the median and 10–90% range of 2000 Haar fiducials per dimension; pink shows the geometric representative α = (1/3)e2πitd from the explicit sufficient IC region, with td = 0 for odd d and td = 1/(4d) for even d. Its analytic upper envelope decays exponentially but does not bound all BICs. (c) Exact balanced-Alltop stability...

FIG. 2. Exact Hilbert–Schmidt MSE ratio R for canonical linear inversion at I/q in prime dimensions. The WH-SIC benchmark is R = 1, and larger R means larger error. Purple circles show balanced Alltop, blue the median and 10–90% range over 4000 Haar fiducials, and pink diamonds the geo- metric representative α = 1/3 from the explicit sufficient IC region (all plotted dimensions are odd). Ratios are evaluated analytically from the nonidentity projector-Gram spectrum and are independent of N; no measurement-shot Monte Carlo is used. For prime q, cyclic and finite-field WH phase spaces coincide.

Figure 2 uses the WH-SIC value R = 1 as its benchmark. Across the displayed primes, the balanced-Alltop ratio decreases from 1.474 to 1.194, whereas the Haar median rises from 3.117 to 6.108 and the geometric representa- tive grows from 8.828 to 3.20 × 106. Thus informational completeness alone does not control this canonical finite- sample linear-inversion MSE, even for the fixed maximally mixed input.
